data.title: Earth Sciences’ Seminar Series - “Multi-Scale Field Remote Sensing for Rock Mass Characterization and Rock Slope Stability: Case Studies from British Columbia” - Sina Fatolahzadeh
Distinguished Lecture Series
data.summary:
Title: Lessons from Safety Engineering for Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence

Abstract: The methodologies of safety engineering have produced highly-reliable systems in aviation, power and water infrastructure, and many other high-risk applications. This talk will review standard safety engineering methodology and extensions that have been introduced by Nancy Leveson and others. It will then consider several implications for machine learning and artificial intelligence including the following:

  • we need methods that can provide formal, distribution-independent guarantees for machine learning methods
  • we need improved methods for detecting anomalies and near miss events
  • we need to design AI systems to include continuous human oversight

The talk will analyze current failures and challenges in autonomous systems that have been deployed without meeting these requirements including self-driving cars, cyber security agents, and programming agents. The talk with close with a discussion of the implications for self-improvement and loss of control in “frontier” AI systems.

data.title: Geoff Winsor | PhD Thesis Defence, MBB
data.summary:
Lay Abstract:
Asthma is the most common chronic disease among children, and finding ways to reduce the risk of developing it could reduce its impact on children and the healthcare system. The CHILD Cohort Study has followed 3,454 healthy Canadian children and their families from early pregnancy, collecting data on their health, lifestyle, home environment and neighbourhood, while collecting biological samples for analysis. Compared with other studies, CHILD captures substantial diversity reflecting Canadian demographics, and detailed exposure datasets from many early time points in life. Centralizing these datasets would offer the capability of performing more sophisticated analyses while also addressing shortcomings that negatively impact other cohort studies. First, I describe how integration of CHILD data into a database called CHILDdb, and integration of additional data generated from biological samples, can help researchers investigate relationships between early-life exposures and childhood asthma development. Secondly, I used CHILDdb data to examine nearly 3000 exposures occurring between pregnancy and the first 5 years of life for later associations with asthma and recurrent wheeze occurring between ages 1 and 8 years. Several exposures were associated with asthma, including antibiotic use, high human milk fatty acid and phthalate levels, and maternal prenatal cleaning product and disinfectant use. Even if the mother halted cleaning product exposure after birth, associations between prenatal cleaning product use and asthma remained. Among girls, higher adrenic acid in breast milk was associated with asthma. Next, a complementary machine learning approach identified similar exposures as the previous analysis. It also identified additional exposures and interactions between family asthma history, prenatal cleaning product use, and air pollution. Lastly, frequent prenatal cleaning product use was associated with changes in cord blood DNA methylation, suggesting clues for how maternal prenatal exposures contribute to asthma development. Other exposures were associated with changes in the gut bacteria and blood proteins (cytokines) of the immune system. These findings support asthma as a complex and varied disease with multiple potential mechanisms leading to its development. The results could also lead to identifying potential exposures that could be targeted for future research into interventions that could reduce childhood asthma risk.
